content.problem: A course script may contain CPU-specific device selection or assumptions that do not transfer to TPU. Before staging, classify the exact script as CPU-only, single-host accelerator-compatible, multi-host-qualified, or not yet reviewed. Multi-host discovery is a topology receipt; it is not evidence of distributed training.
content.idea: Use a per-script execution matrix. `distributed-02` is CPU-only because it explicitly selects CPU devices; route it to CPU. Treat other scripts as unreviewed until their exact source, backend selection, dependencies, topology assumptions, and data ownership are checked. Existing bounded receipts cover the v5e1 checkpointed launcher and precision target and the four-device single-host collective target; each is limited to its named source and configuration. Multi-host requires simultaneous worker launch and initialization, followed by distinct process-owned inputs and a checked global update. Keep discovery receipts separate from training receipts.
objectives: Classify each course script as CPU-only, review-required, single-host-compatible, or multi-host-qualified before staging.
Keep CPU-only `distributed-02` on CPU; do not infer compatibility for Transformers, Pallas, or other lessons.
Generate a TPU command only for a source-reviewed target with an explicit backend assertion, pinned dependencies, known topology, and data-ownership contract.
Distinguish `--worker=all` process discovery from a multi-host program with verified global data and collective updates.

sections.title: Why every worker must launch and initialize
sections.body: A multi-host collective is a coordinated computation: every participating process must initialize and enter the same named collective. The lesson's small update assumes one valid example per device and equal local device counts, so an average of local means equals the global mean. If valid counts differ, reduce gradient sums and counts separately, then divide once by the total count. A successful `--worker=all` launch only shows that workers started; retain each process receipt and check input ownership and the global update before calling it training evidence.

check.prompt: If a TPU slice has `hosts = 4` and `chips_per_host = 4` (`v5litepod-16`), what are `jax.local_device_count()` and `jax.device_count()` on each host after `jax.distributed.initialize()`?
check.answer: `jax.local_device_count()` is `4` (the chips attached to that host VM), while `jax.device_count()` is `16` (all chips across all 4 hosts in the Pod slice).

sections.math: g_{\text{global}} = \frac{\sum_{p=0}^{P-1} n_p g^{(p)}}{\sum_{p=0}^{P-1} n_p}; \qquad \text{this fixture assumes } n_p=1 \text{ valid example per device and equal devices per host}

sections.title: 1. Route a script using the execution matrix
sections.body: Route the exact source, not a lesson category. `distributed-02` selects CPU, so run it on CPU and keep its CPU receipt. The v5e1 launcher, precision target and four-device single-host collective each have separate, bounded receipts for their named sources, environments and layouts; those receipts do not qualify a different script. Before staging another program, inspect its backend selection and dependencies, then specify process/device topology and which process owns each input. Generate a TPU command only when those checks are complete.

sections.title: 2. Separate multi-host discovery from a qualified training run
sections.body: The discovery command launches all workers and calls `jax.distributed.initialize()`. This is a discovery check only: it reports the global topology but does not prove that data was partitioned correctly, that gradients were globally reduced, or that a checkpoint can be recovered. The one-step example below is an executable teaching program, not a reported TPU result. A real multi-host claim needs a named slice, simultaneous initialization, distinct process-owned inputs, independently checked global update values, synchronized checkpoint evidence and a receipt from every worker. The recorded sixteen-device v5e checkpoint run is separate: it used `resources/tpu-gcp/multihost_target.py` and its own receipts; it does not qualify this example.

commands.label: Record multi-host process and device discovery only
commands.code: gcloud compute tpus tpu-vm ssh "$TPU_NAME" --zone="$ZONE" --worker=all --command="set -euo pipefail; JAX_PLATFORMS=tpu ~/jax-tpu-lab/.venv/bin/python -c 'import jax; jax.distributed.initialize(); print(dict(process=jax.process_index(), process_count=jax.process_count(), global_devices=jax.device_count(), local_devices=jax.local_device_count()))'"
commands.expected: Each worker reports process and device counts. This verifies topology discovery only; it does not establish data ownership, a collective training update, or checkpoint recovery.

commands.label: Run a one-step multi-host collective update after discovery
commands.code:
cat > ./multihost_collective.py <<'PY'
import json
import os
from pathlib import Path
from functools import partial
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np
from jax.experimental import multihost_utils

jax.distributed.initialize()
process_index = jax.process_index()
process_count = jax.process_count()
local_devices = jax.local_device_count()
# Each process owns one valid scalar example per local device; all processes must have equal local device counts for this equal-count mean.
x_local = jnp.full((local_devices,), float(process_index + 1), dtype=jnp.float32)
@partial(jax.pmap, axis_name="devices")
def update(theta, x):
    local_grad = 2.0 * (theta - x)
    # Equal-count fixture: one valid example per device, so global device count is also the global valid-example count.
    global_mean_grad = jax.lax.psum(local_grad, "devices") / jax.device_count()
    return theta - 0.1 * global_mean_grad, global_mean_grad

theta0 = jnp.zeros((local_devices,), dtype=jnp.float32)
theta1, grad = update(theta0, x_local)
jax.block_until_ready((theta1, grad))
expected_mean_gradient = -float(process_count + 1)  # assumes every process contributes one example per local device and local counts match
expected_theta = 0.1 * float(process_count + 1)
if not np.allclose(np.asarray(grad), expected_mean_gradient):
    raise RuntimeError("global reduction does not match the independently derived mean gradient")
if not np.allclose(np.asarray(theta1), expected_theta):
    raise RuntimeError("updated parameter does not match the expected global update")
if not np.allclose(np.asarray(theta1), np.asarray(theta1)[0]):
    raise RuntimeError("replicas produced different parameter updates")

out_dir = Path(os.environ.get("TPU_RUN_DIR", "~/jax-tpu-lab/multihost-run")).expanduser()
out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
receipt = {"process_index": process_index, "process_count": process_count,
           "local_devices": local_devices, "global_devices": jax.device_count(),
           "owned_input": float(process_index + 1),
           "global_mean_gradient": float(np.asarray(grad)[0]),
           "updated_theta": float(np.asarray(theta1)[0]),
           "backend": jax.default_backend()}
(out_dir / f"worker-{process_index}.json").write_text(json.dumps(receipt, sort_keys=True) + "\n")
# Publish a single checkpoint only after all workers finish the same collective update.
multihost_utils.sync_global_devices("after-global-update")
if process_index == 0:
    tmp = out_dir / "checkpoint.json.tmp"
    tmp.write_text(json.dumps({"theta": receipt["updated_theta"], "global_devices": jax.device_count()}, sort_keys=True) + "\n")
    os.replace(tmp, out_dir / "checkpoint.json")
print(json.dumps(receipt, sort_keys=True))
PY
gcloud compute tpus tpu-vm scp ./multihost_collective.py "$TPU_NAME":~/jax-tpu-lab/ --zone="$ZONE" --worker=all
gcloud compute tpus tpu-vm ssh "$TPU_NAME" --zone="$ZONE" --worker=all --command="set -euo pipefail; mkdir -p ~/jax-tpu-lab/multihost-run; export TPU_RUN_DIR=~/jax-tpu-lab/multihost-run; JAX_PLATFORMS=tpu ~/jax-tpu-lab/.venv/bin/python ~/jax-tpu-lab/multihost_collective.py | tee ~/jax-tpu-lab/multihost-run/stdout-\$(hostname).jsonl"
commands.expected: Each process writes a worker-indexed receipt with its distinct input, global gradient, updated parameter, and observed backend. The independent expected values are mean gradient = -(process_count + 1) under the one-example-per-device, equal-local-device-count assumption and updated theta = 0.1 * (process_count + 1); these checks reject a local-only reduction. Process 0 publishes checkpoint.json after the global barrier. Treat these as TPU results only after running on and naming a multi-host slice.

buildSteps.title: Tabulate single-host and multi-host TPU slice topologies
buildSteps.instruction: Create main.py with SLICE_CATALOG and compute global_chips, total_hbm_gib, and multi_host.
buildSteps.code:
# Step 1 — Tabulate single-host and multi-host TPU slice topologies
import json
import jax
import numpy as np

SLICE_CATALOG = [
    {"slice": "v5litepod-4", "hosts": 1, "chips_per_host": 4, "hbm_per_chip_gib": 16},
    {"slice": "v5litepod-8", "hosts": 1, "chips_per_host": 8, "hbm_per_chip_gib": 16},
    {"slice": "v5litepod-16", "hosts": 4, "chips_per_host": 4, "hbm_per_chip_gib": 16},
    {"slice": "v6e-16", "hosts": 4, "chips_per_host": 4, "hbm_per_chip_gib": 32},
]
for entry in SLICE_CATALOG:
    entry["global_chips"] = entry["hosts"] * entry["chips_per_host"]
    entry["total_hbm_gib"] = entry["global_chips"] * entry["hbm_per_chip_gib"]
    entry["multi_host"] = entry["hosts"] > 1
buildSteps.explanation: Separating hosts from chips_per_host shows immediately when a slice crosses the single-host boundary into multi-host execution.

experiments.title: Compare local vs global device counts across slices
experiments.prediction: How many global chips are left idle if you launch a script without `--worker=all` on `v5litepod-16`?
experiments.code:
# Experiment — Compare local vs global device counts across slices
v5e16 = next(s for s in SLICE_CATALOG if s["slice"] == "v5litepod-16")
idle_without_worker_all = v5e16["global_chips"] - v5e16["chips_per_host"]
print("v5litepod-16 global chips:", v5e16["global_chips"], "Idle chips without --worker=all:", idle_without_worker_all)
# Assert invariant `idle_without_worker_all == 12` holds
assert idle_without_worker_all == 12
experiments.output: Without `--worker=all`, 12 of the 16 TPU chips on `v5litepod-16` never receive a process.
experiments.explanation: Worker 0 only controls its own 4 local chips; the other 3 hosts (`3 * 4 = 12` chips) require `--worker=all`.

experiments.title: Verify total HBM scaling from v5litepod-16 to v6e-16
experiments.prediction: How much total HBM is available across a 16-chip `v6e-16` Pod slice compared to `v5litepod-16`?
experiments.code:
# Experiment — Verify total HBM scaling from v5litepod-16 to v6e-16
hbm_by_slice = {s["slice"]: s["total_hbm_gib"] for s in SLICE_CATALOG}
print("Total HBM GiB by slice:", hbm_by_slice)
assert hbm_by_slice["v6e-16"] == 512 and hbm_by_slice["v5litepod-16"] == 256
experiments.output: v6e-16 provides 512 GiB of total HBM across 4 hosts (32 GiB/chip), double v5litepod-16's 256 GiB (16 GiB/chip).
experiments.explanation: Doubling per-chip HBM on Trillium (`v6e`) doubles the total sharded model state capacity for the same 4-host Pod topology.

practice.prompt: If each TPU chip processes a microbatch of \(8\) sequences on `v5litepod-16` (`4` hosts, `4` chips/host), compute the per-host batch size and the global batch size per step.

content.question: You launch an ordinary TPU-VM SSH command on worker zero of a multi-host slice, without another launcher. What can happen?
options: Google Cloud automatically merges the 4 Linux hosts into 1 host
Only that worker starts the command; distributed initialization or collectives can wait for the missing participants
The script runs four times faster
content.explanation: An explicit launcher must start every participating process with compatible configuration. --worker=all is one Cloud TPU API method; other orchestrators can do the same job. Initialization, data ownership and collected worker receipts still require separate checks.
content.diagnosis: If `gcloud compute tpus tpu-vm ssh --worker=all` fails on one worker because `.venv` is missing, run your `.venv` bootstrap command with `--worker=all` as well so every host has `~/jax-tpu-lab/.venv` installed.
takeaways: Keep `distributed-02` on CPU. Before staging another script, inspect its exact backend selection and dependencies, assert the TPU backend and topology, and document which process owns each input.

Every hardware receipt applies to its exact source, environment, devices and workload. `--worker=all` provides a launch mechanism; training and recovery need their own checked global updates and complete worker receipts. The recorded sixteen-device checkpoint test is separate from this lesson's one-step example.

visual.title: Host count, per-host local chips, and global TPU chips across single-host and Pod slices
visual.prediction: How do `hosts`, `chips_per_host`, and `global_chips` change when moving from `v5litepod-4` and `v5litepod-8` to `v5litepod-16` and `v6e-16`?
visual.reading: The horizontal axis lists four requested slices. The three bars per slice count VM hosts, local chips per host and global physical chips. `v5litepod-4` has 1 host × 4 chips = 4 global chips; `v5litepod-8` has 1 × 8 = 8. `v5litepod-16` and `v6e-16` each have 4 hosts × 4 local chips = 16 global chips. The host and chip counts are different units of topology, so read each bar series by its legend. The decision boundary is hosts: at four hosts, launch all workers and initialize distributed JAX; then verify local and global JAX device counts in each receipt.
visual.connection: The slice calculation shows why `--worker=all` is required for the two 16-chip, four-host layouts; it is not evidence that a workload trained across them. In a 4-host example with 4 local chips per host, the expected topology is 4 local chips and 16 global chips per host process, subject to the selected API's runtime mapping. Keep the CPU rehearsal and recorded target receipts separate, and require per-process receipts plus a checked global update before claiming multi-host training.
